[votes a1: 1, a3: 2] A. Maintainer tests
- `test_parsing_rfc850` directly exercises `parse_http_date()` with an RFC 850 date containing a two-digit year (likely the existing `94` example) and checks the parsed date/year. All three candidates accept the same call signature and can be exercised by this test.
- `test_parsing_year_less_than_70` directly exercises `parse_http_date()` with an asctime date whose year is `0037`, checking that the existing interpretation remains 2037. Candidates 1 and 3 retain the legacy rule for this non-RFC850 format; candidate 2 also retains it because the year token has four characters. None prevents this test from calling the parser.

B. Reported scenarios
The issue and comments require interpreting RFC850 two-digit years relative to the current year, not with the fixed 00–69/70–99 split. A year whose same-century candidate is more than 50 years in the future must roll back a century; one exactly 50 years ahead must not. The thread specifically mentions the `69` regression case, the boundary case (for example, `68` versus `69` with a fixed 2018 clock), and pinning the clock in tests; it also raises using UTC rather than local time. The equivalent boundary in 2026 is `76` staying in 2076 and `77` rolling to 1977. Candidates 1 and 3 explicitly apply the rule only to RFC850 matches. Candidate 2 produces the same results for all currently accepted two-digit-year inputs, since RFC850 is the accepted format with a two-character year, but expresses the condition by token length rather than format.

C. Newly failing tests
All candidates report zero newly failing tests. There is therefore no newly failing repository test that contradicts the requested behavior. In particular, the existing year-less-than-70/asctime behavior is retained by all three.

D. Weighing the patches
All three use the UTC current year and apply the correction by default at the year-interpretation point in `parse_http_date()`, so callers receive the fix without API changes. Candidates 1 and 3 key the behavior directly to the matched RFC850 pattern, matching the scope of the RFC requirement and leaving other formats on their existing path. Candidate 2 is correct for the present regexes, but its length-based condition is less explicit about the format to which the RFC rule applies. Candidates 1 and 3 are behaviorally equivalent: candidate 1 records which regex matched, while candidate 3 checks `m.re` directly. I prefer candidate 3 because it directly tests the pattern that produced the match and keeps the RFC850-specific condition at the point where the year is interpreted. It fixes the root cause and leaves unrelated date-format behavior and output unchanged.

[votes a2: 3] A. Test coverage and candidate callability
- `test_serialize_class_based_validators` most likely calls `MigrationWriter.serialize()` on class-based validators and asserts the serialized validator expression and imports. A validator such as `RegexValidator` contains a `re.RegexFlag`, which reaches `EnumSerializer` while serializing its arguments. It needs no new keyword or option; all three candidates accept the same serialized value.
- `test_serialize_enums` most likely calls `MigrationWriter.serialize()` on enum members and enum-containing field definitions, asserting generated expressions and imports. The candidates all accept these values without extra arguments.

B. Reported broken scenarios
The issue and comments describe a translated lazy enum value (for example, `Status.GOOD = _('Good')`) used as a `CharField` default. The generated `Status('Good')` lookup can fail after the translation changes the value; the simpler reproduction is the same pattern with `EnumClass.VALUE = _('Value')`, followed by generating migrations and running them under another language. All three candidates serialize named members through their stable names, so all fix the reported cases. They also retain value-based serialization for unnamed flag combinations, which have no usable declared member name.

C. Newly failing tests
The reported failures are old expected-output assertions: `test_serialize_enums` expects `TextEnum('a-value')`, and `test_serialize_class_based_validators` expects `re.RegexFlag(16)`. Both assert the old value-based enum serialization that this issue asks to change. The enum test should expect name lookup; the validator test should likewise expect the named `RegexFlag` member. These are not negatives for any candidate, though maintainers would need to update the expectations.

D. Comparison
All candidates fix the root cause in `EnumSerializer`, apply by default wherever named enum members are serialized, preserve imports, and produce the requested `EnumClass['NAME']` form. Candidates 1 and 3 use the same membership test. Candidate 2 additionally verifies that looking up the name returns the exact member being serialized. That check avoids emitting a lookup to a different member in an unusual enum implementation, without changing behavior for normal named members, aliases, or the reported case. It is therefore the safest correct implementation while covering the same reported scenarios.

E. Best choice
Candidate 2.

[votes a2: 3] A. Maintainer tests and whether each patch supports them

- `test_non_blank_foreign_key_with_radio` (`ModelFormBaseTest`) most likely builds a ModelForm for a `blank=False` ForeignKey with `RadioSelect`, then checks that the empty choice is absent and that a new form has no checked radio. All three candidates can affect this path: candidate 1 passes the model’s `blank` value into `ModelChoiceField`; candidate 2 relies on the generated field being required; candidate 3 sets `empty_label=None` in `ForeignKey.formfield()`.
- `test_choices_radio_blank` (`ModelChoiceFieldTests`) most likely exercises a ModelChoiceField’s choice list with a radio widget, checking whether the blank choice is present for required versus optional fields. Candidate 2 can handle this directly using `required` and the widget. Candidate 1 can handle it only if the test supplies its new `blank=False` argument; a normal required ModelChoiceField call defaults to `blank=True` and retains the empty choice. Candidate 3 only changes the ForeignKey formfield path, so it cannot fix a direct ModelChoiceField choices test.
- `test_clean_model_instance` (`ModelChoiceFieldTests`) directly calls `ModelChoiceField.clean()` with a model instance, most likely asserting that a valid instance is returned (and possibly that an instance of the wrong model is rejected). None of the patches changes cleaning, and all can still construct and call the field for this test.

B. Reported broken scenarios

The issue’s concrete case is a new ModelForm for a `null=True, blank=False` ForeignKey rendered with `RadioSelect`: it includes a checked `"---------"` radio even though blank is invalid. The requested behavior is to omit that option, leaving the radio choices unselected. The issue contrasts this with ordinary Select widgets, for which retaining a blank choice is idiomatic; it does not ask to alter their output. No further comment text or additional broken scenario is provided here. The choices-level maintainer test also favors handling the underlying ModelChoiceField radio-choice behavior, not just one rendering path. Candidate 2 covers both the ForeignKey case and direct required ModelChoiceField radio choices. Candidate 1 covers the ForeignKey case but does not cover a direct required ModelChoiceField unless callers pass its added `blank=False` argument. Candidate 3 covers the ForeignKey case only.

C. Newly failing tests

All candidates report no newly failing repository tests, so there is no newly failing behavior to discount as an intentional test change.

D. Comparison

Candidate 2 changes the source of the empty option, `ModelChoiceField.empty_label`, and uses the field’s existing `required` semantics: a required single-select radio field gets no empty choice, while optional fields and ordinary Select widgets retain existing behavior. This matches the model-form mapping from `blank=False` to `required=True` and also covers the choices-level test. It handles widget classes and instances and avoids changing cleaning or unrelated output.

Candidate 1 also addresses the reported ForeignKey case, but introduces a separate `blank` parameter into ModelChoiceField and passes it through ForeignKey formfield construction. That duplicates the existing `required` signal, leaves direct required radio fields unchanged by default, and risks passing a new keyword to custom form classes supplied through `ForeignKey.formfield()`.

Candidate 3 is appropriately localized for the reported ForeignKey rendering, and preserves explicit `empty_label` overrides, but does not change direct ModelChoiceField radio choices. That makes it a weaker fit for `test_choices_radio_blank` and the underlying field behavior.

Candidate 2 is the best match for the reported behavior and the likely coverage of all three maintainer tests.

[votes a1: 1, a3: 2] A. Test call sites and candidate compatibility
- `test_clash_parent_link` most likely constructs models with parent-link and clashing relations, then calls Django’s model checks (`Model.check()` or the relevant relation-clash checks) and asserts the expected clash diagnostics. All three patches are in `ModelBase`, accept the same model declarations, and can be exercised by this test; none changes the check API.
- `test_onetoone_with_parent_model` most likely constructs an MTI child with a OneToOneField targeting its parent and asserts which field becomes the parent link, or whether the ordinary relation remains independent. All three can be called by it. Candidate 2 handles the case where an explicitly marked link competes with another field, but not a lone unmarked OneToOneField to the parent; candidates 1 and 3 do handle that ordinary, non-primary-key case.

B. Reported broken scenarios
- With `document_ptr` marked `parent_link=True` before `origin`, the later ordinary OneToOneField overwrites it, causing Django to demand `parent_link=True` on `origin`.
- Reversing the fields happens to work, so declaration order changes the result.
- Adding `primary_key=True` to the actual pointer can suppress the immediate configuration error, but the model can still be broken: the wrong field may be treated as the inheritance link and the parent pointer ID is not populated on save.
- The follow-up simpler case has only an ordinary `some_unrelated_document = OneToOneField(Document, ...)` on the child. It produces the same erroneous missing-parent-link error even though that relation is intended to be independent.

Candidates 1 and 3 fix the original order-dependent selection and the simpler ordinary, non-primary-key case by not letting an unmarked field displace an explicitly marked link (or stand in for it when no candidate is appropriate). Candidate 2 fixes the competing-fields order issue, but still selects a lone unmarked OneToOneField and raises the error in the simpler reported case.

C. Newly failing repository test
Candidates 1 and 3 newly fail `test_missing_parent_link`, which is exactly the old expectation that an unmarked OneToOneField to the parent must raise. The simpler follow-up report says this is erroneous behavior, so this should be changed by maintainers and is not a negative for those candidates. Candidate 2 avoids that failure only because it retains the behavior the issue reports as broken; it may therefore fail the updated `test_onetoone_with_parent_model` expectation.

D. Choice
Candidate 3 is the best fit. It fixes the field-order root cause by giving `remote_field.parent_link` precedence, and it leaves the ordinary non-primary-key relation out of parent-link discovery, addressing the follow-up report. Its primary-key fallback also accommodates the primary-key variant discussed in the comments. Candidate 1 fixes the reported examples too, but additionally treats any auto-created OneToOneField as a parent-link candidate even when it is not marked; that fallback is unnecessary for the reported behavior and can reintroduce the same mistaken selection for an unmarked auto-created relation. Candidate 2 is insufficient because it does not fix the standalone ordinary OneToOneField case.

[votes a2: 1, a3: 2] A. Maintainer tests and whether the candidates can serve them

- `test_autoclass_content_and_docstring_signature_init` most likely builds autodoc output with `autoclass_content='init'` and docstring-signature extraction enabled. It exercises the class documenter’s choice of constructor documentation and its signature formatting, then asserts the rendered signature/content. - `test_autoclass_content_and_docstring_signature_both` most likely exercises the same path with `autoclass_content='both'`, asserting how class and constructor docstrings/signatures are selected and combined. Again, it does not directly call the private parser or require a changed keyword. All three candidates can be called by it. The reports say these tests pass for all three.

B. Reported broken scenarios

The issue first reports SWIG-wrapped C++ classes with overloaded Python methods, where the overload signatures are placed at the beginning of the docstring and `autodoc_docstring_signature` extracts only the first. The follow-up gives the concrete Qt case: `getFeatures` has four overloads, and the generated documentation shows the four signatures together with the four docstrings. The requested behavior is to recognize all leading overload signatures, not just the first. The comments do not establish a separate simpler reproducer beyond clarifying this four-overload case.

All three candidates recognize consecutive leading signature lines with valid names, remove the recognized lines from the body, and emit multiple signatures. Thus all address the reported core scenario; candidates 2 and 3 route each signature through the normal formatter, while candidate 1 constructs the additional output separately.

C. Newly failing tests

There are no newly failing repo tests reported for any candidate. Consequently, there is no reported failure here to classify as either an intentional change to behavior described in the issue or a strong negative.

D. Comparison against the requested behavior

All three preserve the existing `autodoc_docstring_signature` setting as the gate and only extract a signature when no explicit signature was supplied. They work at the parsing/formatting cause of the issue rather than applying a later rendering workaround, and they leave the ordinary single-signature path broadly intact.

Candidate 1 is weaker because it formats only the first signature through `super().format_signature()` and manually formats the rest, including a separate event call. That risks diverging from the normal formatter’s behavior for additional signatures, despite the hook call. It also does not retain the parsed list for a later formatting call.

Candidate 2 formats every extracted signature through the normal formatter and preserves the old `_find_signature` helper as a first-signature compatibility path. That is a useful compatibility detail. However, after formatting it restores `self.args` to the first signature; a later call to `format_signature()` then skips extraction because `self.args` is no longer `None`, and emits only that first signature. It does not cache and reuse the overload list for that case.

Candidate 3 also sends each signature through the normal formatter, so each follows the existing formatting and signature-event path. Its cached `_docstring_signatures` list lets later calls continue to emit all overloads after `self.args` has been restored to the first signature. It changes the private `_find_signature` return shape from one pair to a list and updates its internal caller, which is a compatibility cost, but the listed tests do not call that helper directly. For the requested multi-signature formatting behavior, its cache avoids candidate 2’s repeat-call loss.

E. Choice

Candidate 3 most completely implements the requested default behavior while reusing normal signature formatting for every overload. Its private-helper API change is less important here than correctly retaining the overloads across formatting calls. Independent summaries and test reports are not decisive evidence; the behavior in the diffs is the basis for this choice.
